english: Verse 25: “May the stars walk about in his dwellings.” They are in ignorance, for they cast the light away from themselves—the ones to whom he said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Verse 20: “Unquenchable fire will devour him.” According to the hidden sense, unquenchable fire is either the fire of conscience or the fire stored up in the coming courts of judgment. “And he will be consumed as by fire,” he says, so as to say: He is not even deemed worthy of burial. Verse 29: “This is the portion of an impious man from the Lord, and the possession of his goods from the overseer.” According to this, the divine judgment is set in motion against him. Whether it is the one from the circumcision who acted impiously toward God through Christ, or the one who is impious in some strange way, or however he may be impious, this is the portion described for him. Learn who is named overseer here: God is called overseer, and the good and noble overseers strive in every way to bear his image. And just as the one who imitates a royal image is honored for imitating it well—and is honored also for having adorned it—so too blessed is the overseer who has understood the true overseer, and who zealously imitates him, and who becomes as God among human beings; or blessed is the one who has an overseer who truly makes him an overseer in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.

Chapter 21, verses 11–12: “Their children play, taking up harp and lyre, and they rejoice with the sound of a psalm.” See how even their foolish children play among themselves. For they sing the psalms of Valentinus and the odes of Basilides, and they utter things of that kind, rejoicing with the sound of a psalm.

Chapter 22, verse 2: “Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” Let us see what Eliphaz says to the righteous man: “Is it not…” and so on. Since Job has said this, Eliphaz agrees with his word and says: I too know that the words by which one man who is impious is set straight and another is punished—only the wise God knows these. And I know this too: that God, as you yourself said, is the giver of good things, but vice gives the punishments. The doctrine is sound. Knowledge is the comprehension of things that remain the same, and understanding is discernment.

Verse 5: “Is not your vice great, and are not your sins without number?” Reasonably, then, I say that you have not simply become unjust, since you suffer such things as none of the wicked suffer; rather, you were born in these things, which clearly means you have had greater vice than the others. Vice is a bad disposition in the soul, such as of grief, anger, and improper desire; sin is the activity. Therefore he first said vice, then sin—the one great, the others without number. I see very many sinners, and none of them has fallen into such great things as you. For it is likely that because of the countless number of your sins and the multitude of your transgressions, these things have come upon you.

Verse 6: “You took pledges from your brothers without cause, and you stripped the clothing of the naked.” Let us pay attention, we moneylenders, lest we ever take pledges without cause. The words are useful, in that they speak truly of sins that are committed among human beings in a blameworthy way. Eliphaz supposes this about Job because he knew he was rich, and he suspected that he had become rich from such sources. Therefore he says: “You took pledges without cause,” that is, when nothing was owed to you. If I lent money and, not trusting the borrower, took a pledge worth what I lent, I took a pledge, but not without cause. If, however, I slander someone and say he owes me when he cannot repay, and I demand and take, I take a pledge without cause.

He presses further again, thinking that another sin of his has occurred. It is possible sometimes to take clothing, not from the naked, but from a rich man who has other garments stored away—many garments to take, three indeed. Of those many garments there I took clothing. One thing is the clothing of the naked, another the clothing of the rich. If, however, someone has one tunic, and I strip that tunic from him under the pretext of demanding what is mine, without pitying that naked man, I have taken the clothing of the naked. Many such things happen among us when we lend, when we go to debtors. Often our debtor is exceedingly poor and cannot repay, and we shut up our hearts and become merciless and cruel, not seeing that he feeds a wife and children and barely feeds himself from the few coins he earns. We demand bitterly, sometimes even when we have more than enough ourselves.
